title: API 510 Training in Billings, MT: Vessel Inspector Exam Prep
description: API 510 exam prep for Billings and Laurel vessel inspectors: self-paced online with instructor Q&A, built around Montana refineries, crude and winter work.
h1: API 510 Training in Billings, Montana: Online Exam Prep for Refinery Pressure Vessel Inspectors
html:
API 510 exam prep for vessel inspectors at the Yellowstone refineries

Few cities the size of Billings hold this much refining. EIA's capacity survey for the start of 2026 lists two refineries inside the city and a third at Laurel, west of town along the Yellowstone River: Phillips 66's plant at 71,000 barrels per calendar day of crude distillation, Par Montana's at 61,500 and the CHS refinery, listed as Cenex Harvest States, at 62,500. Between them they run crude columns, coker fractionators, hydroprocessing reactors, amine and sulfur plant vessels and a long list of drums, all of which need inspection to a recognised code.

The Atlantis NDT course prepares you for the API 510 Pressure Vessel Inspector examination. It is self-paced and online, an instructor answers your questions while you work through it, and you begin the day you enrol. There is no Atlantis classroom in Billings. The American Petroleum Institute decides eligibility, administers the examination in person at Prometric test centres and certifies those who pass.

Three refineries, three ways of converting heavy oil

The plants are close in crude capacity but not in design, and design decides which vessels an inspector meets. The table uses the EIA survey for the start of 2026, which gives crude distillation in barrels per calendar day (b/cd) and the downstream units in barrels per stream day (b/sd).

Refinery (owner in the EIA survey)Crude and vacuumMain downstream units, b/sdVessels that follow
Phillips 66 Company, Billings71,000 b/cd crude; 52,000 b/sd vacuumDelayed coking 20,050; catalytic cracking 24,900; high-pressure reforming 9,700; hydrotreating of jet 25,000, diesel 32,300 and heavy gas oil 29,380; hydrogen 50 MMcfd; sulfur 325 short tons a dayCoke drums, FCC reactor and regenerator, hydrotreater reactors, amine and sulfur vessels
Par Montana LLC (Par Pacific), Billings61,500 b/cd crude; 32,300 b/sd vacuumFluid coking 10,000; catalytic cracking 23,660; distillate hydrocracking 6,200; high-pressure reforming 12,500; hydrotreating of naphtha 13,900, gasoline 20,500, jet 7,600 and diesel 11,000; asphalt 14,500; hydrogen 23 MMcfdFluid coker reactor and burner, FCC vessels, hydrocracker reactors and separators
Cenex Harvest States Coop (CHS), Laurel62,500 b/cd crude; 32,200 b/sd vacuumDelayed coking 16,000; catalytic cracking 16,500; low-pressure reforming 12,500; hydrotreating of naphtha 17,000, other distillate 24,500 and heavy gas oil 20,000; asphalt 19,800; hydrogen 70 MMcfd; sulfur 243 short tons a dayCoke drums, FCC vessels, hydrotreater reactors, hydrogen and sulfur plants

Read the table as a guide to the job, then check it against the exam. Coke drums are the most distinctive vessels in the valley, but the thermal fatigue they are known for is not among the RP 571 sections the current API 510 Body of Knowledge examines. Erosion and erosion-corrosion (RP 571 section 3.27) is listed, and the fluid coker and catalytic crackers, with their circulating solids, are prone to it. The hydroprocessing reactors bring high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion (3.35) and high-temperature hydrogen attack (3.36), both examined, and the amine and sulfur units bring amine stress corrosion cracking (3.3) and wet H2S damage (3.67).

Montana inspects boilers, not unfired pressure vessels

Montana's boiler statute, Title 50, chapter 74 of the Montana Code Annotated, covers boilers and steam engines. It tells the Department of Labor and Industry to adopt rules for them that follow ASME standards, and it lets the department commission the inspectors of authorised boiler insurance companies as special boiler inspectors, each of whom must hold a National Board certificate, and accept their reports as equivalent to a state inspection. The department's boiler safety rules then state plainly that the statute gives it no jurisdiction over unfired pressure vessels.

That changes where the authority for vessel work comes from. A drum or column at a Billings refinery is not on a state inspection schedule; it is inspected under the owner's mechanical integrity programme. Montana is not an OSHA State Plan state, so federal OSHA's process safety management standard applies to the refineries directly, and its mechanical integrity element wants inspection and testing to follow recognised and generally accepted good engineering practice, more often when operating experience says so. EPA's Risk Management Program rule repeats the requirement for Program 3 processes in 40 CFR 68.73. Refiners commonly meet both by working to API 510, which is why the certificate carries weight in Billings even though the state's boiler rules never reach an unfired vessel.

The reverse also holds: an API 510 certificate does not make anyone a Montana boiler inspector. The state's own inspectors need five years of experience operating or inspecting boilers and the qualifications for a stationary engineer's licence or a National Board commission.

What Canadian and Rocky Mountain crude brings to the vessel list

All three refineries buy crude from Canada as well as from the region. CHS says its Front Range Pipeline carries more than 65,000 barrels a day of crude from the Canadian border to the Laurel and Billings refineries. Par Pacific describes its Billings plant as running Western Canadian and Rocky Mountain crude, and the 70-mile Silvertip pipeline that came with its 2023 purchase gives the refinery direct access to Rocky Mountain grades. When Phillips 66 shut its Billings refinery for a full turnaround in 2017, BIC Magazine reported a mix of heavy, high-sulfur Canadian crude and domestic crudes, and a vacuum improvement project that would let the plant run up to all heavy Canadian crude.

Heavy, sour feed puts sulfur on the vessel list twice. In hot sections, sulfidation (RP 571 section 3.61) thins carbon and low-alloy steels; in the cooler coker, FCC and amine systems, wet H2S blistering, HIC, SOHIC and sulfide stress cracking are what the inspection plan has to find. Crude unit overheads add hydrochloric acid corrosion (3.37). Naphthenic acid corrosion (3.46) is on the examined list as well; whether it matters on a particular Billings crude unit depends on the acid content of the crudes it runs, a question for site process data rather than the exam. For each listed mechanism, learn what makes equipment susceptible, where the damage appears and which method finds it; the course takes every listed section in that pattern.

Winter, brittle fracture and impact testing

A Billings inspector works on vessels in cold weather for a good part of the year, and three parts of the Body of Knowledge speak to it. Brittle fracture (RP 571 section 3.11) is one of the listed mechanisms. The impact testing topic asks you to understand UG-84 testing and to determine the minimum metal temperature at which a material is exempt from impact testing, using UG-20(f), UCS-66 and UCS-68(c). And the pressure testing topic asks you to calculate a test pressure compensating for temperature under UG-99 and UG-100, and to know the precautions that go with hydrostatic and pneumatic tests, minimum test temperatures among them.

On site, those clauses settle winter questions: whether an older drum can be pressure tested on a cold day without warming it, and what a weld repair to a carbon steel shell does to its impact test exemption. They are table and curve exercises, so practise reading UCS-66 in the PDF until you can pick the right curve for a material and its thickness without hunting.

Worked example: which part limits a drum's MAWP?

The Body of Knowledge asks you to work out a vessel's maximum allowable working pressure from the MAWPs of its parts and their elevations, with all static head based on a specific gravity of 1.0, at 0.433 psi per foot. Take a vertical knockout drum with a nameplate MAWP of 225 psi at the top. The shell has an inside radius of 30 in. and a longitudinal seam with a joint efficiency of 0.85. The bottom head is a seamless 2:1 ellipsoidal head of 60 in. inside diameter, so E = 1.0. Allowable stress is 20,000 psi for both. At the last inspection the shell measured 0.420 in. at its lowest point, 30 ft below the top of the vessel, and the head measured 0.380 in., its lowest point 32 ft below the top.

  1. Shell, UG-27(c)(1). P = SEt ÷ (R + 0.6t) = 20,000 × 0.85 × 0.420 ÷ (30 + 0.252) = 7,140 ÷ 30.252 = 236.0 psi at the bottom of the shell. Static head there is 30 × 0.433 = 12.99 psi, so the shell supports 236.0 − 13.0 = 223.0 psi at the top.
  2. Head, UG-32(c). P = 2SEt ÷ (D + 0.2t) = 2 × 20,000 × 1.0 × 0.380 ÷ (60 + 0.076) = 15,200 ÷ 60.076 = 253.0 psi at the bottom of the head. Static head is 32 × 0.433 = 13.86 psi, leaving 239.2 psi at the top.
  3. Vessel. The lower value governs: about 223 psi at the top, two pounds short of nameplate. The thinner head is not the problem, because its formula and seamless joint efficiency leave more margin than the welded shell has.

Check it the other way. The shell's required thickness at 225 + 13.0 = 238.0 psi is PR ÷ (SE − 0.6P) = 238.0 × 30 ÷ (17,000 − 142.8) = 7,140 ÷ 16,857 = 0.424 in., more than the 0.420 in. measured. In corrosive service the rule is stricter again: the ninth edition of API 510 (2006), the edition published at law.resource.org, has you compute MAWP from the measured thickness minus twice the corrosion expected before the next inspection. Confirm the clause in the edition on your effectivity sheet.

Routes into API 510 from Billings jobs

API weighs education and experience together, and the experience must have been gained in the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology, or three years of technical military service, needs one year supervising or performing inspection as the code describes it. A two-year degree or certificate in engineering or technology needs two years in design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of vessels, of which one year is inspection. A high school diploma needs three years on the same terms, and no formal education needs five or more. You document the experience on the application and API verifies it; the API 510 certification requirements page sets the rules out in full.

City College at Montana State University Billings runs an associate degree in process plant technology and lists graduates working at the Billings refineries, at CHS in Laurel and at the refinery in Casper. Operating years help, but the two-year and three-year routes still need a year spent supervising or performing inspection, and whether API treats a particular two-year programme as engineering or technology is API's decision on your application. Its welding and metal fabrication programmes send people into refinery piping and pipeline construction, where repair experience builds and Section IX becomes familiar early. NDT technicians doing thickness readings, shear wave UT, MT and PT on vessels are often closest to the inspection year; see NDT training in Billings for the method certifications behind that work.

Studying for API 510 around a Billings turnaround

Turnarounds here are big events for a small labour market. The 2017 Phillips 66 turnaround shut the whole refinery for almost two months and brought about 2,500 employees and contractors onto the site at its peak, and BIC Magazine reported at the time that the plant went through one every five years. A turnaround is the worst time to study and the best time to collect inspection experience, so plan the course around it.

  • Before the outage. Learn the closed-book material: interval and remaining-life rules, corrosion rate formulas and the listed RP 571 sections. Memory needs quiet weeks.
  • During it. Note which vessels were opened, what was found and how it was dispositioned, and send short questions to the instructor between shifts.
  • After it. Move to the open-book half: timed practice with the Section VIII, Section V and Section IX PDFs, the UW-12 joint efficiency table, UCS-66 and the UG-99 test pressure clause, until finding a paragraph takes seconds.

When API accepts your application you schedule the exam with Prometric. Its online locator shows which test centres have seats in your window; book early if the closest one with space is a long drive from the Yellowstone valley.

Sponsoring vessel inspectors from a Billings refinery, contractor or shop

Refineries, inspection contractors and fabrication shops around Billings can enrol several candidates at once, and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate still applies to API in their own name; the employer's part is usually to confirm experience and plan study around the outage calendar. A sponsor should also budget for keeping the certificate: recertification every three years asks for at least 20% of the last three years spent performing or supervising pressure vessel inspection, 24 continuing professional development hours across at least two categories, and a web-based quiz on code changes every six years. Crews who also need NDT method certification under ASNT SNT-TC-1A can see the NDT training courses.

faq.q: Is there an API 510 preparation class I can attend in person in Billings?
faq.a: Not from Atlantis. There is no Atlantis classroom in Billings or anywhere else; the API 510 course is online and self-paced, with an instructor answering questions, and you can start as soon as you enrol. Whichever way you prepare, the examination is taken in person at a Prometric test centre once API accepts your application.

faq.q: Does Montana require API 510 certification to inspect a refinery pressure vessel?
faq.a: Montana's boiler law covers boilers and steam engines, and the Department of Labor and Industry's rules say the statute gives it no jurisdiction over unfired pressure vessels. Vessel inspection at a Billings refinery is driven instead by the owner's mechanical integrity programme under federal OSHA process safety management and EPA's Risk Management Program, which expect good engineering practice. Most refiners use API 510 for that, so employers ask for the certificate.

faq.q: I am a special boiler inspector in Montana with a National Board commission. Is API 510 still worth adding?
faq.a: It covers different equipment. Your commission lets the state accept your boiler inspections on behalf of an insurance company; API 510 is about in-service inspection, repair, alteration and rerating of unfired pressure vessels in refineries and chemical plants, which Montana's boiler rules do not reach. If your work takes you onto refinery vessels, it is the credential owners look for; check what experience API will accept before applying.

faq.q: Does inspection work on coke drums or the fluid coker count toward API 510 experience?
faq.a: Inspection of pressure vessels as API 510 describes it counts, whatever unit the vessels sit in, provided it was done in the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency and you document it on the application. API verifies the experience and makes the decision. Thermal fatigue in coke drums, though, is not among the RP 571 sections the exam draws on.

faq.q: I graduated from the process plant technology programme at City College and work as an operator. Can I qualify for API 510?
faq.a: Possibly, but operating time alone is not enough. On the two-year and three-year routes API wants experience in design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of vessels that includes at least one year supervising or performing inspection. Whether API counts your associate degree as a two-year programme in engineering or technology is decided on your application. Many operators build that year in an inspection or NDT role.

faq.q: Our refinery's procedures still cite an older API 510 edition. Which edition will I be examined on?
faq.a: The one on the Publications Effectivity Sheet for your exam window. API's Body of Knowledge notes that some organisations and jurisdictions work to other editions, and says plainly that the examination is based on the editions on the effectivity sheet. Study those, and note where they differ from the edition your site uses.

faq.q: Can a Billings inspection contractor enrol several vessel inspectors together?
faq.a: Yes. Employers can sponsor a group, and fees are quoted on request. Each person studies at their own pace and asks the instructor questions individually, which suits crews split across plants and shifts. Every candidate still submits a separate application to API with their own experience record, and each schedules their own exam with Prometric once API has approved it.
